newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai stocks set to fall further near term -brokers.
newsitem.headline: Thai stocks set to fall further near term -brokers.

text.p: The Thai stock market is set to fall further in the short term as foreign investors continue to dump blue chip bank and communications stocks, analysts said.

"I think it is headed much further south...people have given up waiting for the market to recover," said George Morgan, country manager at broker HG Asia and head of Thailand's Foreign Brokers Association.
The key SET Index finished at 876.89 on Friday, its lowest close since June 14, 1993. The index has lost over 100 points since November 27, when it ended at 959.23.
Fears over Thailand's slowing economy and doubts that the new government can remedy the situation continue to rattle investors and dampen market sentiment, analysts said.
Recently-revised figures by the central Bank of Thailand put gross domestic product (GDP) growth for 1996 at around 7.0 percent -- its lowest level for a decade.
In addition export growth slowed to 0.9 percent year-on-year over the first nine months of the year, compared to 24 percent in 1995.
The current account remains stubbornly high at eight percent of GDP, loan portfolio quality is believed by analysts to be deteriorating while corporate profitability has been sluggish.

"In the short term the market will go down further... (foreign) selling pressure has been quite strong in the last few days, it seems they want to get out whatever the cost," said Susheel Narula, head of research at Seamico Securities.
Traders said market confidence in the increasingly fractious coalition government of Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh has steadily waned since coming to power last month.

"It looks as if the new government is already hit by internal conflicts and that is bad news for the economy... investors are no longer prepared to sit in the market and wait for policies," said one trader.
The government will reveal its policies on the economy in parliament on December 11.
But an early government initiative to take 25 basis points off interest rates was poorly received by the market and commercial banks.
Combined with plunging share prices, some investors see the possibility of a devaluation of the local currency.
"I think this is very much a worst case scenario," said HG Asia's Morgan.
"I think priority should be on reassuring international markets that the Finance Ministry and the Bank of Thailand see no reason to devalue the currency and can and will defend it against attack."
Youssef Abboud, an investment analyst at Wall Street Finance, added: "The baht could come under attack if they try to lower interest rates again with the current account this high."
These combined fears have all but killed any hopes of a short-term recovery based on asset allocations by fund managers ahead of the Christmas holiday period.

"All fundamentals and factors do not support a rebound in the market. For appearances at year-end people are thinking they had better unload from the Thai market. If a market is going down prior to a holiday period you don't buy." said Abboud.
